steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package. This will allow you to use React's core functionality and state management in your TypeScript component.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with curly braces to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and useState from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The import statement for React and useState is added at the top of the file.
successCriteria: The code must include a valid import statement that imports both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core library and the useState hook for managing component state in TypeScript.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'. Check that the import statement uses the correct syntax with curly braces.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. Remember to import both React and useState from the 'react' package using the import statement.

steps.title: Define the TemperatureInput props interface
steps.instruction: Create an interface called TemperatureInputProps to define the props that the TemperatureInput component will receive. The interface should have two properties: temperature (string) and onTemperatureChange (function).
steps.hint: Use the TypeScript interface keyword to define the shape of the props. The onTemperatureChange property should be a function that takes a string parameter and returns void.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a TypeScript interface that defines the props structure for the TemperatureInput component, enabling type checking for the temperature and onTemperatureChange props.
successCriteria: The interface should be named TemperatureInputProps and contain two properties: temperature of type string and onTemperatureChange of type (value: string) => void.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the TemperatureInputProps interface with the correct properties and types. This will provide TypeScript type safety for your component props.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your interface has both required properties with the correct types. Make sure temperature is typed as string and onTemperatureChange as (value: string) => void.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition doesn't match the requirements. You need to create an interface named TemperatureInputProps with temperature (string) and onTemperatureChange (function that takes a string and returns void) properties.

steps.title: Apply the props interface to TemperatureInput
steps.instruction: Update the TemperatureInput component to explicitly type its props parameter using the TemperatureInputProps interface you created in the previous step.
steps.hint: Add the type annotation to the component's parameter. For example: `function ComponentName(props: PropsInterfaceName) { ... }`
steps.expectedOutcome: The TemperatureInput component's props parameter is now explicitly typed with the TemperatureInputProps interface, providing type safety for the component.
successCriteria: TemperatureInput component's props parameter is typed with TemperatureInputProps
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully typed the TemperatureInput component's props with the TemperatureInputProps interface. This provides TypeScript type checking for the component's props.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've explicitly typed the TemperatureInput component's props parameter with the TemperatureInputProps interface. Check that you're using the correct interface name and syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The TemperatureInput component's props parameter is not properly typed with the TemperatureInputProps interface. Make sure to add the type annotation to the component's parameter.

steps.title: Add the input field to TemperatureInput
steps.instruction: Inside the TemperatureInput component, return an input element with type='text' and value bound to the temperature prop.
steps.hint: The input element should be the only thing returned from the component. Use JSX syntax: <input type="text" value={temperature} />
steps.expectedOutcome: The TemperatureInput component now renders a text input field that displays the temperature value passed via props.
successCriteria: The component returns a single input element with type='text' and value={temperature}.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully added the input field to the TemperatureInput component. The input will display the temperature value passed from the parent component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your input element. Make sure it has both type='text' and value={temperature} attributes.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on just adding the input element. The TemperatureInput component should return a single <input> element with type='text' and value bound to the temperature prop.

steps.title: Wire the input's onChange event
steps.instruction: Add an onChange event handler to the input element inside your TemperatureInput component. The handler should call a function named onTemperatureChange with the event's target value (e.target.value).
steps.hint: Use the onChange prop on the input element. Pass a function that receives the event and calls onTemperatureChange with e.target.value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The input element will have an onChange handler that calls onTemperatureChange with the current input value.
successCriteria: The input element includes an onChange prop with a function that calls onTemperatureChange(e.target.value).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully wired the input's onChange event to call the onTemperatureChange callback with the current value.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your onChange handler correctly calls onTemperatureChange with e.target.value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The input element needs an onChange handler that calls onTemperatureChange with the event's target value. Check your syntax and ensure you're passing the value correctly.

steps.title: Create the Calculator component
steps.instruction: Create a new functional component named Calculator that will serve as the parent component. The component should return an empty JSX element (like a div) for now.
steps.hint: You can create a component using either a function declaration or arrow function syntax. Make sure it returns JSX.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a Calculator component defined that returns an empty div element.
successCriteria: The code contains a functional component named Calculator that returns JSX (like a div).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the Calculator parent component. This component will manage the shared state for the temperature inputs.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've created a component named Calculator that returns JSX (like a div).
steps.feedbackWrong: The Calculator component isn't properly defined. Create a functional component named Calculator that returns JSX.

steps.title: Initialize temperature state in Calculator
steps.instruction: Inside the Calculator component, declare a state variable called 'temperature' using the useState hook. Initialize it with an empty string.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. The state variable should be a string, so you can use useState<string>('') or let TypeScript infer the type from the initial value.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of declaring a string state variable
const [name, setName] = useState<string>('');
steps.expectedOutcome: The Calculator component now has a temperature state variable that will be shared with child components.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call inside the Calculator component, creating a state variable named 'temperature' initialized to an empty string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the temperature state in the Calculator component. This state will be lifted up and shared with the TemperatureInput component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've properly declared the state variable. Check that you've used useState with an empty string initial value and named the variable 'temperature'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Calculator component doesn't have the temperature state initialized yet. Remember to use the useState hook inside the Calculator component to create a state variable called 'temperature' with an empty string initial value.

steps.title: Define the temperature change handler
steps.instruction: Inside the Calculator component, define a function named handleTemperatureChange that takes a string parameter (newTemperature) and calls setTemperature with that value.
steps.hint: Create a function that updates the state when called. Use the setTemperature function from useState.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Calculator component now has a handler function that can update the temperature state when called.
successCriteria: The code should include a function named handleTemperatureChange that takes a string parameter and calls setTemperature with it.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the handler function that will update the shared temperature state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function takes a string parameter and calls setTemperature with it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handler function isn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function that accepts a string and calls setTemperature with it.

steps.title: Render the first TemperatureInput component
steps.instruction: In Calculator's return statement, render the TemperatureInput component with the temperature state and handleTemperatureChange function passed as props.
steps.hint: Pass the temperature state variable as the temperature prop, and pass handleTemperatureChange as the onTemperatureChange prop to the TemperatureInput component.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Calculator component should render the TemperatureInput component with the temperature state and handleTemperatureChange function passed as props.
successCriteria: TemperatureInput component is rendered with temperature={temperature} and onTemperatureChange={handleTemperatureChange} props.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully passed the shared state and handler down to the TemperatureInput component as props. This is the core pattern of lifting state up.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you're passing both the temperature state and the handleTemperatureChange function as props to TemperatureInput.
steps.feedbackWrong: The TemperatureInput component needs to receive both the temperature state and the handler function as props. Make sure you're passing temperature={temperature} and onTemperatureChange={handleTemperatureChange}.

steps.title: Render the second TemperatureInput component
steps.instruction: In the Calculator component's return statement, add a second TemperatureInput component with the same temperature and onTemperatureChange props as the first one.

steps.expectedOutcome: The Calculator component will render two identical TemperatureInput components side by side, both receiving the same props.

Both components receive the same temperature prop

steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a second TemperatureInput component. This demonstrates how lifted state can be shared by multiple child components.
